iconic_games_note: BC Place has a genuine major-football pedigree: it was a principal venue of the 2015 FIFA Women's World Cup, hosting the Final (USA 5–2 Japan, 5 July 2015, attendance 53,341) plus multiple group/knockout matches. It is the first Canadian venue confirmed for a men's World Cup (2026), hosting 7 matches: 5 group-stage (incl. host nation Canada), one Round of 32 (July 2) and one Round of 16 (July 7). Non-football landmark events also include serving as the main stadium for the 2010 Winter Olympics and Paralympics (opening/closing ceremonies). 2026 knockout opponents are TBD pending group results.

renovations.change: Installed a natural-grass (hybrid sod) pitch for the tournament, replacing BC Place's usual FieldTurf synthetic surface as mandated by FIFA. Custom Kentucky bluegrass / perennial ryegrass blend, cultivated in the Fraser Valley and laid on a specialized base. Pitch built toward FIFA 2-star certification. Confirmed installed per BC government release.

city_history.significance: Vancouver is the largest city in British Columbia and the third-largest metropolitan area in Canada — a major Pacific port and gateway on Canada's west coast, ringed by the North Shore Mountains and the Pacific Ocean. It was the host city of the 2010 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games, whose ceremonies were staged at BC Place.
city_history.football_culture: Vancouver has one of Canada's deepest soccer roots. Organized association football was played in British Columbia from the early 1900s (the Pacific Coast Association Football League formed in 1908, first pro game 1910). The Vancouver Whitecaps won the NASL's Soccer Bowl in 1979, drawing roughly 100,000 fans to a Robson Street victory parade; the 86ers (named for 1886, the city's founding) carried the lineage through the 1980s–90s, and the modern Whitecaps FC joined MLS in 2011, playing at BC Place. Vancouver also hosted the 2015 FIFA Women's World Cup Final at BC Place, cementing the city as a major Canadian football hub.

sources.title: History of Vancouver Whitecaps FC — Wikipedia

stadium_history_facts: Opened 19 June 1983; originally the world's largest air-supported domed stadium, with an inflatable fabric roof.
Original construction cost CA$126.1 million (~CA$356M in 2025 dollars).
Owned by the Province of British Columbia and operated by the BC Pavilion Corporation (PavCo).
Underwent a ~16-month, ~CA$514 million revitalization completed in 2011 that replaced the inflated dome with a retractable cable-supported roof — the largest of its kind in the world.
Home of the BC Lions (CFL) since 1983 and Vancouver Whitecaps FC (MLS) since 2011; also hosts Canada Sevens rugby and the BC Sports Hall of Fame.
Served as the main stadium for the 2010 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games (opening/closing ceremonies).
Hosted the 2015 FIFA Women's World Cup Final (USA 5–2 Japan, 5 July 2015, attendance 53,341), among other WWC matches.
Soccer pitch dimensions 117 × 75 yards (107 × 69 m); targeting FIFA 2-star certification.
Features the second-largest centrally-hung high-resolution scoreboard in North America (after AT&T Stadium).
